x.A: DataSync securely moves the existing data to S3 over the network with encryption and integrity checks. CloudTrail data events log object-level access, which gives the audit access at all levels the regulation asks for.
x.B: Snowcone holds little data, and CloudTrail management events record only control-plane actions, not object-level access.
x.C: Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads but isn't built to migrate existing on-premises data. The CloudTrail data events part is right.
x.D: Storage Gateway can move data to S3, but logging only management events misses object-level (data) access.

x.A: Lambda can't host a complex Java application that must run on Apache Tomcat without a rewrite.
x.B: Elastic Beanstalk supports Java on Tomcat, and a load-balanced environment with a rolling deployment keeps the application highly available. It also manages the platform for you.
x.C: ElastiCache is an in-memory cache, not a replacement for a MySQL database.
x.D: A single EC2 instance with MySQL on it is a single point of failure, and the Auto Scaling group wouldn't keep database data consistent.

x.A: An IAM user with access keys stored in environment variables means long-term credentials in the function configuration, which is less secure.
x.B: A role that trusts the Lambda service, with a policy allowing read and write access to the table, used as the function's execution role gives temporary credentials automatically. It's the most secure way.
x.C: Keys in Parameter Store still involve long-term credentials, and the code has to retrieve them.
x.D: A role must trust Lambda (the service that assumes it), not DynamoDB, so this is incorrect.

x.A: The policy has a Deny statement that applies too, and policy statements aren't ignored after an Allow. Evaluation checks every statement.
x.B: Only stopping and terminating instances are denied without MFA. Other EC2 actions are allowed in us-east-1.
x.C: The Allow covers only us-east-1, so permissions aren't granted for all Regions.
x.D: The first statement allows all EC2 actions in us-east-1. The second denies StopInstances and TerminateInstances unless MFA is present, so those two actions need MFA, and other EC2 actions are allowed only in us-east-1.

x.A: A Spot Instance polling hourly isn't as fast as event-driven conversion, and it needs a server to manage.
x.B: A Lambda function invoked when a .csv file is uploaded converts it right away and costs nothing when idle, so the images are available as soon as possible.
x.C: The .csv files must be kept for ML training twice a year, planned weeks in advance, so slow retrieval from Glacier is acceptable and it's the cheapest. Image files expire after 30 days.
x.D: One Zone-IA costs more than Glacier for data that is rarely used and stores in a single AZ, so it's less cost-effective for files kept long term.
x.E: Standard-IA costs more than Glacier for rarely accessed data, and Reduced Redundancy Storage is a legacy class that isn't recommended.

x.A: Memcached can cache scores but has no sorted data structures or persistence, so it can't compute a top 10 or restore scores after a stop.
x.B: ElastiCache for Redis has sorted sets that compute a leaderboard in near real time, and its persistence lets the game be stopped and restored with scores preserved.
x.C: CloudFront caches content at the edge but can't compute the scoreboard or preserve scores.
x.D: A read replica still runs queries on the database, so it isn't near real time and has no persistence advantage for a leaderboard.

x.A: A Glue ML transform is for tasks like deduplication, not for building and training general ML models, and OpenSearch isn't a BI dashboard tool.
x.B: SageMaker builds, trains, and deploys ML models as a managed service, and QuickSight connects to the results for BI dashboards, with little operational overhead.
x.C: An ML AMI on EC2 means managing instances and software, which is more operational overhead.
x.D: QuickSight calculated fields aren't for building and training ML models.

x.A: A Config rule detects and flags noncompliant tag changes after they occur. It doesn't prevent the modification.
x.B: CloudTrail records API calls and can't prevent them.
x.C: An SCP applied through Organizations can deny tag-modifying actions for everyone except authorized principals, so the change is blocked across accounts.
x.D: CloudWatch Logs can't prevent actions, since it only stores logs.

x.A: A second Region with an Auto Scaling group and load balancer already running, a DynamoDB global table that keeps data in sync, and Route 53 DNS failover gives the least downtime, because the stack is ready.
x.B: Launching everything from a CloudFormation template only when needed takes time to build, and it also leaves out the data, so downtime is longer.
x.C: Launching the EC2 instances and load balancer on demand takes time, so downtime is longer than with a running stack.
x.D: A manual-style alarm and Lambda to update Route 53 is more custom work than built-in DNS failover and adds delay.

x.A: A Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device carries the 20 TB offline, and DMS with SCT captures ongoing changes, so the final cutover has minimal downtime. It's much cheaper than Snowmobile or a dedicated connection.
x.B: Snowmobile is for exabyte-scale transfers and is far too large and expensive for 20 TB.
x.C: A Compute Optimized with GPU device is built for edge compute, not for storing and shipping data cost-effectively.
x.D: A dedicated Direct Connect connection takes weeks to provision and costs more for a one-time migration, so it can't meet 2 weeks.

x.A: A larger DB instance handles more workload without adding infrastructure, and reserved DB instances for the total workload lower the price for steady use. It's the most cost-effective.
x.B: Multi-AZ improves availability but doesn't increase capacity for the workload, because the standby doesn't serve traffic.
x.C: Adding another DB instance adds infrastructure, which the company wants to avoid, and a second instance wouldn't share the workload by itself.
x.D: On-Demand pricing is more expensive than reserved pricing for a steady database, and it doesn't add capacity.

x.A: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities and can't be associated with an ALB or block requests.
x.B: AWS WAF on the ALB with a rate-based rule blocks IP addresses that send too many requests, even when the IPs change, and legitimate users with normal request rates aren't affected.
x.C: Network ACLs filter by IP address range and can't keep up with changing IP addresses, and they can't use request rates.
x.D: GuardDuty detects threats and doesn't have rate-limiting protection.

x.A: A read replica with IAM database authentication gives the auditor connection access to the live database, but doesn't give them their own copy in their account.
x.B: Exporting to text files and sharing S3 access creates unprotected copies and uses IAM users, which is less secure.
x.C: Sharing IAM user keys is insecure, and it's not the way to share a snapshot.
x.D: An encrypted snapshot shared with the auditor's account, with access to the KMS key, lets them restore their own copy securely, without moving the data over the internet.

x.A: A VPC can have additional IPv4 CIDR blocks added. Adding one and creating new subnets gives more IP addresses with little work.
x.B: A second VPC with peering needs route updates and splits the environment, so it's more operational work.
x.C: A transit gateway adds another service to manage and extra cost for the same purpose.
x.D: A VPN between two VPCs on EC2 is complex and costly to run.

x.A: You can create an Aurora MySQL DB cluster directly from an RDS for MySQL snapshot, so the snapshot can be imported straight into Aurora.
x.B: There's no need to upload an RDS snapshot to S3 first, and RDS snapshots can't be exported that way for this purpose.
x.C: A mysqldump file can be uploaded to S3 and loaded into Aurora, for example by using the MySQL client, so the dump is a valid source.
x.D: DMS doesn't import an RDS snapshot.
x.E: DMS migrates from a live source database and doesn't import a dump file.

x.A: Reserved Instances lower the price of the servers but don't change why so many instances are launched for static content.
x.B: Spot Instances can be interrupted, and the application would still use servers to serve static content.
x.C: CloudFront serving the static content from S3 removes that load from the EC2 instances, so fewer instances are needed. It's the cheapest way to serve static files.
x.D: Hosting static content behind API Gateway and Lambda costs more than S3 and CloudFront.

x.A: Copying petabytes of data into a common account is slow and costly, and it creates duplicates.
x.B: Granting permissions with the Grant command in each account is manual per account and doesn't scale.
x.C: AWS Data Exchange is for sharing data products with external subscribers, and it's heavier than needed for internal sharing.
x.D: Lake Formation tag-based access control lets you grant cross-account permissions on selected data using tags, without copying data, and it scales with little overhead.

x.A: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads and downloads of large objects to and from users around the world, with no servers to manage, so it is cost-effective and high-performing for gigabyte-sized files.
x.B: CacheControl headers affect caching of downloads and don't speed up uploads, and S3 alone isn't an application host.
x.C: CloudFront caches downloads, but unique data uploaded by users isn't cached, and EC2 adds cost and servers.
x.D: ElastiCache doesn't minimize upload and download latency for large files, and EC2 adds cost.

x.A: Deleting an EC2 instance reduces availability, and a single instance in one AZ is a single point of failure.
x.B: Multi-AZ with deletion protection guards the database against failures and accidental deletion, and an ALB with an Auto Scaling group across AZs makes the web tier highly available.
x.C: A second database fed by Lambda and API Gateway is a complicated design that doesn't provide automatic failover or protect against deletion.
x.D: Spot Instances can be interrupted, which reduces reliability.

x.A: A DataSync agent in the data center transfers the data over the 10 Gbps Direct Connect, with scheduling and verification, while users keep accessing and updating the NAS. It can finish within 90 days.
x.B: Snowball Edge devices don't let you keep updating the data during the transfer, because the data copy is a point in time, and mounting a bucket on the on-premises file system isn't how it works.
x.C: rsync to S3 isn't supported directly and lacks the management and verification that DataSync has.
x.D: Tapes are slow, and mounting an S3 bucket on the on-premises file system isn't how tape restores work.

x.A: Versioning with MFA Delete doesn't prevent deletion by authorized users in all cases, and doesn't enforce the 7 year retention for existing data.
x.B: Governance mode can be bypassed by users with permission, so it doesn't strictly meet a legal retention requirement, and recopying every object is a lot of work.
x.C: Compliance mode is right, but recopying all existing objects is manual work compared with Batch Operations.
x.D: Compliance mode with a 7 year retention period can't be shortened or removed by anyone. S3 Batch Operations applies the retention to all existing objects in one job, so it needs the least work.

x.A: Route 53 health checks with an active-active configuration route traffic to healthy Regional API endpoints and remove a Region when it fails. It's simple and fits a stateless application.
x.B: CloudFront with multiple origins can use origin groups for failover, but it's not what the question describes, and health checks on origins aren't done that way.
x.C: A transit gateway can't attach to API Gateway endpoints and doesn't route requests.
x.D: An ALB's target group can't point to API Gateway endpoint hostnames in other Regions.

x.A: VPNs between the two VPCs aren't needed, because VPC peering already connects them, and it doesn't remove the data center link's single point of failure.
x.B: A second virtual private gateway can't be attached to the same VPC, because a VPC can have only one.
x.C: The Management VPC connects to a single device in the data center through VPNs. A second set of VPNs from a second customer gateway device removes that single point of failure.
x.D: A VPC peering connection is already a redundant, highly available construct, so a second one doesn't improve resilience.

x.A: RDS for Oracle doesn't give privileged OS or database access for third-party features, so they'd have to be replaced, which takes time and effort.
x.B: RDS Custom for Oracle gives access to the database and OS needed for the third-party features while AWS manages backups and maintenance, so it fits the limited admin resources and is cost-effective.
x.C: Oracle on EC2 gives access, but the company would have to manage backups, patching, and the OS, which it lacks resources for.
x.D: Rewriting the application for PostgreSQL takes a lot of time, which doesn't fit a quick migration.

x.A: Keeping the existing three-tier architecture on one instance per AZ doesn't separate the tiers, so it doesn't follow best practices for scalability and resiliency.
x.B: A single RDS database isn't resilient, since a failure would take the data layer down.
x.C: Separating the web, application, and database tiers into their own private subnets across two AZs, with Auto Scaling for the web and application tiers, follows Well-Architected practice.
x.D: A single RDS database isn't resilient, even if access is restricted.
x.E: Load balancers in front of the web tier, with security groups that reference each layer's security group, gives secure, scalable access.
x.F: A Multi-AZ RDS cluster in private subnets, reachable only from the application tier's security groups, makes the database tier secure and highly available.
